 "sourceFile":"The deceleration deficit - A novel field-based method to quantify deceleration during change of direction performance.pdf",
 "decision":"DEGRADED",
 "exclusionReason":"",
 "degradedReason":"The article's own DOI is not printed in the extracted text (no DOI in the header, footer or citation line). Operator may verify externally. All other fields are complete.",
 "doiMissing":true,
 "identityCheck":"Title in text is 'The Deceleration Deficit: A Novel Field-Based Method to Quantify Deceleration During Change of Direction Performance', matching the filename.",
 "confidence":"high",
 "studyDesign":"Cross-sectional Study",
 "primaryDomain":"Monitoring & Technology",
 "domains":["Monitoring & Technology","Training & Performance"],
 "audiences":["Performance","Athletic Training","Research & Analytics"],
 "sports":["Mixed / General Sport"],
 "populations":["Female Athletes","Male Athletes","Healthy Athletes","Adult / Recreational"],
 "evidenceSummary":"Cross-sectional study of 36 recreationally active athletes (19 women, 17 men; mean age 20.3 years) who competed in invasion sports and were free from injury and illness. Each completed three 505 change-of-direction trials in each turning direction and three 15 m linear sprints. Linear speed correlated with 505 time (r = 0.71 to 0.76), but not with the change of direction deficit (CODD) or the new deceleration deficit (DD). DD correlated with CODD (r = 0.59 dominant, 0.62 non-dominant), and 78% of athletes had a CODD and DD difference greater than the moderate worthwhile change in at least one turning direction.",
 "screeningLimitations":"The sample was small and drawn from mixed invasion sports, and DD was not tested for validity or reliability against force-plate or other criterion measures. The study cannot show what drives DD or whether DD predicts change of direction performance over time.",
 "synthesisCaution":"Staff could treat DD as a validated measure of deceleration ability, when the authors state that its validity and reliability still need testing and that most of its variance is not explained by the measures examined.",
 "paper":{
   "year":2022,
   "citation":"Clarke R, Read PJ, De Ste Croix MBA, Hughes JD. The deceleration deficit: a novel field-based method to quantify deceleration during change of direction performance. Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research. 2022;36(9):2434-2439.",
   "doi":"",
   "abstract":"Examined relationships between linear sprint, 505 change of direction time, change of direction deficit (CODD) and a new deceleration deficit (DD) in 36 athletes who performed 505 trials in both turning directions and 15 m sprints. Linear speed correlated with 505 time but not with CODD or DD, DD correlated moderately with CODD, and most athletes had a worthwhile difference between the two deficit measures.",
   "tldr":"The deceleration deficit is a field-based way to separate braking ability from linear speed in the 505 test. Coaches may find it useful for individualising training, but it still needs validity and reliability testing.",
   "methods":"Cross-sectional design in which participants completed three 505 trials in each turning direction and three 15 m linear sprints in one session. DD was calculated as full approach time in the 505 minus the 15 m sprint time, and CODD as 505 time minus 10 m sprint time. Pearson correlations and within-person z-score comparisons with a moderate worthwhile change threshold were used.",
   "findings":"Linear 10 m and 15 m sprint times correlated with 505 time (dominant r = 0.71 and 0.74; non-dominant r = 0.76 and 0.75; all p < 0.01). Linear sprint times were not significantly related to CODD or DD. DD correlated with CODD (dominant r = 0.59, non-dominant r = 0.62; both p < 0.01). Of the participants, 78% had a difference between CODD and DD z-scores greater than the moderate worthwhile change in at least one turning direction.",
   "limitations":"The authors state that DD requires validity and reliability testing and that the correlations are small to moderate, so only about 20% of DD variance is shared with the other measures. The methods describe participants as recreationally active, while the discussion calls them competitive university-level athletes. Sample size was small and drawn from mixed invasion sports, and DD was not compared against force-plate measures.",
   "practicalImplications":"Coaches could compare DD with CODD to see whether an athlete's change of direction time is limited by braking or by linear speed in each turning direction. The 505 test and a 15 m sprint can be done with timing gates, but DD should be checked with reliability testing in the squad before it guides individual programmes.",
   "athleteDev":"Performance Application: Coaches can use DD alongside linear speed and CODD to decide whether an athlete needs braking work or linear speed work, and to compare the two turning directions. The study used a single session with recreationally active athletes, so the measure should be retested in the specific sport and squad before it shapes individual training targets.",
   "rtp":"Return to Sport Application: The study did not include injured athletes or any return-to-play measures, so it cannot be used to judge readiness to return after injury or to set return-to-sport criteria for braking or change of direction."
 }
}

Pearson correlations and within-person z-score comparisons with a moderate worthwhile change threshold were used.",

"findings":"Linear 10 m and 15 m sprint times correlated with 505 time (dominant r = 0.71 and 0.74; non-dominant r = 0.76 and 0.75; all p < 0.01). Linear sprint times were not significantly related to CODD or DD. DD correlated with CODD (dominant r = 0.59, non-dominant r = 0.62; both p < 0.01). Of the participants, 78% had a difference between CODD and DD z-scores greater than the moderate worthwhile change in at least one turning direction.",

-   "limitations":"The authors state that DD requires validity and reliability testing and that the correlations are small to moderate, so only about 20% of DD variance is shared with the other measures. The methods describe participants as recreationally active, while the discussion calls them competitive university-level athletes. Sample size was small and drawn from mixed invasion sports, and DD was not compared against force-plate measures.",

+   "limitations":"The authors state that DD requires validity and reliability testing, and that most of its correlations with other measures were below r = 0.5, so most of DD's variance is not explained by them. The methods describe participants as recreationally active, while the discussion calls them competitive university-level athletes. Sample size was small and drawn from mixed invasion sports, and DD was not compared against force-plate measures.",

"practicalImplications":"Coaches could compare DD with CODD to see whether an athlete's change of direction time is limited by braking or by linear speed in each turning direction. The 505 test and a 15 m sprint can be done with timing gates, but DD should be checked with reliability testing in the squad before it guides individual programmes.",

"athleteDev":"Performance Application: Coaches can use DD alongside linear speed and CODD to decide whether an athlete needs braking work or linear speed work, and to compare the two turning directions. The study used a single session with recreationally active athletes, so the measure should be retested in the specific sport and squad before it shapes individual training targets.",

"rtp":"Return to Sport Application: The study did not include injured athletes or any return-to-play measures, so it cannot be used to judge readiness to return after injury or to set return-to-sport criteria for braking or change of direction."

 "id":"Q52",
 "sourceFile":"The deficits of isometric knee flexor strength in lengthend hamstring position after hamstring strain injury.pdf",
 "decision":"INCLUDE",
 "exclusionReason":"",
 "degradedReason":"",
 "doiMissing":false,
 "identityCheck":"Title in text is 'The deficits of isometric knee flexor strength in lengthened hamstring position after hamstring strain injury', matching the filename (filename spelling 'lengthend' is a typo).",
 "confidence":"high",
 "studyDesign":"Cross-sectional Study",
 "primaryDomain":"Rehabilitation & Return to Sport",
 "domains":["Rehabilitation & Return to Sport","Sports Medicine & Injury"],
 "audiences":["Rehabilitation","Sports Medicine","Athletic Training"],
 "sports":["Soccer","Rugby","Baseball / Softball","Track & Field","Other Sport"],
 "populations":["Male Athletes","Injured Athletes","Healthy Athletes","Collegiate"],
 "evidenceSummary":"Cross-sectional laboratory study of 14 male college athletes with a self-reported history of hamstring strain injury (HSI) and 14 without. Isometric knee flexor peak torque and rate of torque development were measured at 30, 60 and 90 degrees of knee flexion with the hip at 85 degrees. In the HSI group, peak torque was lower in the previously injured limb at 30 degrees (P = 0.037, d = 0.55) but not at 60 or 90 degrees, and no between-limb differences were found in rate of torque development or hamstring flexibility.",
 "screeningLimitations":"Injury history was self-reported and mostly undiagnosed, time since injury ranged from 1 month to 7 years, and only men were studied. The design is cross-sectional, so the deficit cannot be shown to be a cause or a consequence of HSI, or to predict reinjury.",
 "synthesisCaution":"Staff could read the lengthened-position deficit as a proven reinjury risk marker, when the authors say prospective studies are needed to confirm whether it predicts reinjury.",
 "paper":{
   "year":2022,
   "citation":"Nara G, Samukawa M, Oba K, et al. The deficits of isometric knee flexor strength in lengthened hamstring position after hamstring strain injury. Physical Therapy in Sport. 2022;53:91-96.",
   "doi":"10.1016/j.ptsp.2021.11.011",
   "abstract":"Compared isometric knee flexor peak torque and rate of torque development at 30, 60 and 90 degrees of knee flexion, and hamstring flexibility, between the limbs of 14 male athletes with a history of hamstring strain injury and 14 controls. Peak torque was lower in the previously injured limb at 30 degrees only, and rate of torque development and flexibility did not differ between limbs.",
   "tldr":"Athletes with a past hamstring strain still had lower isometric knee flexor strength in the injured leg, but only when the hamstring was stretched at 30 degrees of knee flexion. Rate of torque development did not differ between legs.",
   "methods":"Cross-sectional laboratory study. Participants with a history of HSI (self-reported, all returned to full training) and controls had isometric knee flexor peak torque and rate of torque development measured on an isokinetic dynamometer at 30, 60 and 90 degrees of knee flexion, seated with the hip at 85 degrees. Hamstring flexibility was measured with the active knee extension test. Analysis used two-way repeated-measures ANOVA with Bonferroni post-hoc tests.",
   "findings":"In the HSI group, peak torque in the injured limb was lower than in the uninjured limb at 30 degrees (P = 0.037, d = 0.55), with no difference at 60 or 90 degrees. Peak rate of torque development showed no limb differences at any angle, and active knee extension did not differ between limbs. The control group showed no between-limb differences in peak torque.",
   "limitations":"Injury was self-reported and mostly not diagnosed by a physician, so injury location and severity are unknown, and 64% of participants had no rehabilitation. Only male athletes were studied, time since injury varied from 1 month to 7 years, and four participants' injured side was non-dominant. The design is cross-sectional, and hip extensor activity and muscle architecture were not measured.",
   "practicalImplications":"Isometric knee flexor testing with the hip flexed and the knee at 30 degrees may show strength deficits that a standard hip-neutral or 0-degree test could miss. Isometric training at a lengthened hamstring range can be started early in rehabilitation, with pain monitored, as the authors suggest. Rate of torque development did not differ between legs, so it did not add information in this sample.",
   "athleteDev":"Performance Application: Strength staff can use a 30-degree isometric knee flexor test with the hip flexed to check between-leg strength in athletes with prior hamstring strain, and include lengthened-position isometric work in their hamstring programme. The study measured strength only, with no sprint or match performance outcomes, so it does not show that these changes improve on-field performance.",
   "rtp":"Return to Sport Application: The study shows that some athletes who have returned to full training still have lower isometric knee flexor strength at a lengthened hamstring position, so testing at that angle could be added to return-to-sport review. It cannot set a return-to-sport cut-off, because the design is cross-sectional and does not show that the deficit predicts reinjury."
 }
}

1	The Delayed Presentation of Achilles
2	Tendon Ruptures Is Associated With
3	Marked Alterations in the Gene Expression
4	of COL1A1, MMPs, TIMPs, and IL-6
5	Niklas Nilsson,*y MD, PhD, M.D. Abdul Alim,z PhD, Franciele Dietrich-Zagonel,z PhD,
6	Sebastian Concaro,*y MD, PhD, Annelie Brorsson,*§ PT, PhD,

8	Investigation performed at the Institute of Clinical Sciences, Sahlgrenska Academy,
9	University of Gothenburg, Gothenburg, Sweden
10	
11	Background: Both acute and chronic Achilles tendon ruptures are affected by alterations in the extracellular matrix during the
12	healing process of the tendon. Yet, these alterations in gene expression patterns are not well characterized.
13	Purpose: To characterize temporal and spatial differences in gene expression patterns after an Achilles tendon rupture and to
14	evaluate if cells from chronic Achilles tendon ruptures have the same ability to form new tendon tissue (tendon constructs) as
15	healthy tendon cells.
16	Study Design: Controlled laboratory study.
17	Methods: A total of 35 patients with surgically treated Achilles tendon ruptures were included in the study and divided into 3
18	groups: acute (\4 weeks), short-term chronic (1-6 months), and long-term chronic (.6 months). Biopsy specimens were col-
19	lected during surgical repair and were used to analyze the gene expression within the different groups and to compare mRNA
20	levels in the proximal and distal tendon ends. A complementary in vitro experiment was performed to evaluate if cells from chronic
21	Achilles tendon ruptures can form tendon constructs.
22	Results: The mRNA levels for COL1A1 and COL3A1 were significantly higher in the short-term chronic group compared with the
23	acute group (P \ .05). Both MMP-1 and MMP-13 had the highest mRNA levels in the acute group (P \ .01) compared with the
24	long-term chronic group, while MMP-2 had the highest mRNA level in the short-term chronic group. Significant differences
25	between the proximal and distal tendon ends were only detected for the monocyte and macrophage marker CD163 (P \ .05),
26	which was more expressed proximally. Cells extracted from chronic Achilles tendon ruptures displayed a similar ability and effec-
27	tiveness to form tendon constructs as healthy tendon cells.
28	Conclusion: A high collagenase gene activity after an Achilles tendon rupture indicated possible rapid matrix degradation in the
29	acute phase. Chronic ruptures appeared to initiate the healing process even before treatment, indicated by the higher expression
30	of collagen in the short-term chronic group. Cells from chronic Achilles tendon ruptures also displayed an ability to form new ten-
31	don tissue in vitro.
32	Clinical Relevance: The study shows a rapid increase in collagenase gene expression, which could lead to matrix degradation
33	that continues for months after an Achilles tendon rupture.
34	Keywords: Achilles tendon rupture; RT-PCR; mRNA levels; chronic Achilles tendon rupture; tissue samples; gene expression

The Delayed Presentation of Achilles
Tendon Ruptures Is Associated With
Marked Alterations in the Gene Expression
of COL1A1, MMPs, TIMPs, and IL-6
Niklas Nilsson,*y MD, PhD, M.D. Abdul Alim,z PhD, Franciele Dietrich-Zagonel,z PhD,
Sebastian Concaro,*y MD, PhD, Annelie Brorsson,*§ PT, PhD,
Katarina Nilsson Helander,*y MD, PhD, and Pernilla Eliasson,*z|| PhD
Investigation performed at the Institute of Clinical Sciences, Sahlgrenska Academy,
University of Gothenburg, Gothenburg, Sweden

Background: Both acute and chronic Achilles tendon ruptures are affected by alterations in the extracellular matrix during the
healing process of the tendon. Yet, these alterations in gene expression patterns are not well characterized.
Purpose: To characterize temporal and spatial differences in gene expression patterns after an Achilles tendon rupture and to
evaluate if cells from chronic Achilles tendon ruptures have the same ability to form new tendon tissue (tendon constructs) as
healthy tendon cells.
Study Design: Controlled laboratory study.
Methods: A total of 35 patients with surgically treated Achilles tendon ruptures were included in the study and divided into 3
groups: acute (\4 weeks), short-term chronic (1-6 months), and long-term chronic (.6 months). Biopsy specimens were col-
lected during surgical repair and were used to analyze the gene expression within the different groups and to compare mRNA
levels in the proximal and distal tendon ends. A complementary in vitro experiment was performed to evaluate if cells from chronic
Achilles tendon ruptures can form tendon constructs.
Results: The mRNA levels for COL1A1 and COL3A1 were significantly higher in the short-term chronic group compared with the
acute group (P \ .05). Both MMP-1 and MMP-13 had the highest mRNA levels in the acute group (P \ .01) compared with the
long-term chronic group, while MMP-2 had the highest mRNA level in the short-term chronic group. Significant differences
between the proximal and distal tendon ends were only detected for the monocyte and macrophage marker CD163 (P \ .05),
which was more expressed proximally. Cells extracted from chronic Achilles tendon ruptures displayed a similar ability and effec-
tiveness to form tendon constructs as healthy tendon cells.
Conclusion: A high collagenase gene activity after an Achilles tendon rupture indicated possible rapid matrix degradation in the
acute phase. Chronic ruptures appeared to initiate the healing process even before treatment, indicated by the higher expression
of collagen in the short-term chronic group. Cells from chronic Achilles tendon ruptures also displayed an ability to form new ten-
don tissue in vitro.
Clinical Relevance: The study shows a rapid increase in collagenase gene expression, which could lead to matrix degradation
that continues for months after an Achilles tendon rupture.
Keywords: Achilles tendon rupture; RT-PCR; mRNA levels; chronic Achilles tendon rupture; tissue samples; gene expression

1201	ACM risk score is available at http://ACMrisk.com [96, 97, 98].
1202	
1203	TREATMENT
1204	
1205	Restriction of exercise activity is extremely important in the management of individuals with ACM
1206	because restriction of exercise intensity and duration significantly decreases the amount of ventricular
1207	dysrhythmias. Athletes with ACM should be restricted to low level activity such as 30 minutes of brisk
1208	walking per day, because exercise levels >650 MET-hours per year accelerate the phenotypic
1209	expression of ACM [99-101]. Exercise restriction should also be advised in athletes and in family
1210	members who are genotype positive but phenotype negative in order to delay potential phenotypic
1211	expression and should also be considered in athletes with borderline or possible ACM [91,102, 103].
1212	
1213	  The use of beta-adrenergic receptor antagonists is recommended in athletes with ACM and non-
1214	sustained ventricular tachycardia or other ventricular dysrhythmias [91]. Adjuvant pharmacotherapy
1215	with flecainide or amiodarone should be considered in athletes with ongoing ventricular dysrhythmias
1216	despite the use of a beta-adrenergic receptor antagonist [104]. However, therapy with beta adrenergic
1217	receptor antagonists, flecainide, amiodarone or ventricular ablation of endocardial/epicardial
1218	ventricular tachycardia foci does not obviate the need for ICDs in high risk athletes as determined by
1219	the ACM risk score [91, 99, 105, 106]. For athletes with asymptomatic but significant RV and/or LV
1220	 reduction in ejection fractions, treatment with angiotensin-converting-enzyme inhibitors or angiotensin
1221	II receptor blockers should also be considered [99].
1222	
1223	  The decision to insert an ICD in an athlete for primary preventions requires thorough evaluation of
1224	the risk of sudden cardiac death and the risk of ICD device-related complications, which include a 3.9%
1225	annual rate of shocks and a 4.2% annual rate of complications such as infection or lead malfunction
1226	[107]... In those athletes with a 5% to 15% 5-year risk with a history of aborted cardiac arrest or sudden
1227	cardiac death, sustain ventricular tachycardia, severe RV, LV or biventricular dysfunction, an ICD is
1228	indicated [99, 108, 109]. In those athletes with intermediate risk with >1 major risk factor such as
1229	syncope, non-sustain ventricular tachycardia, moderate ventricular dysfunction, an ICD should be
1230	considered. In those athletes with >I minor risk factors, an ICD may be considered and in those
1231	athletes with <5% 5-year risk, an ICD is not recommended [99, 108, 109]. For athletes undergoing ICD
1232	implantation for primary prevention of ventricular dysrhythmias, a subcutaneous ICD should be
1233	considered whereas for athletes who present with sustained monomorphic VT, an endocardial ICD
1234	device should be considered because of the risk of recurrent sustained dysrhythmias. Finally, athletes
1235	with uncontrollable ventricular tachydysrhythmias or intractable heart failure require evaluation for
1236	heart transplantation [110].
1237	
1238	Athletes with ACM require reevaluation every one to two years for new onset or worsening of
1239	symptoms, progression of ventricular myocardial abnormalities, and supraventricular and ventricular
1240	dysrhythmias. In these athletes, the risk of sudden cardiac arrest/death should be re-assessed and
1241	treatment further optimized [99].
1242	
1243	
1244	
1245	ATHLETES WITH IMPLANTABLE CARDIOVERTERS-DEFIBRILLATORS (ICDs)
1246	
1247	In individuals of all ages with cardiac disease at high risk for ventricular dysrhythmias, ICDs are
1248	effective in preventing ventricular dysrhythmias and sudden cardiac arrest [84, 107-109, 111-113].
1249	However in the past the AHA/ACC guidelines have recommended against all moderate and high-
1250	intensity sports for athletes with ICDs because the safety and efficacy of these devices during sport
1251	competition was unknown. Recently, studies have reported that athletes primarily with HCM or long
1252	QT syndrome with LV ejection fractions in the normal or the mildly reduced range may be able to
1253	participate safely in noncontact or low contact competitive sports with a low risk of life-threatening
1254	events [113-116]. In these studies appropriate, as well as inappropriate shocks due to T-wave over-
1255	sensing, supraventricular or sinus tachycardia, and lead malfunction, have been reported. A limitation
1256	of some of these studies is that ICD shocks have been self-reported by the athletes or their care givers
1257	and these individuals may have purposefully withheld information about ICD shocks in order to
1258	continue sports participation. Nevertheless, the AHA/ACC currently has Class II recommendations for
1259	athletes with ICDs where participation in sports may be considered if the risk of adverse outcomes
1260	appears to be low or disease-specific management may reduce the risk to acceptable levels [117,118].
1261	 In addition, the European Association of Preventive Cardiology recommends that return to play
1262	decisions be made after thorough discussion and shared decision making by the physician(s) with the
1263	athlete with the ICD, the interested parties (care providers, coaches, institutions and/or organizations)
1264	of the “four Ds”:   (1) the underlying cardiac disease; (2) the danger to the athlete, third parties
1265	involved, and the environment; (3) the device; and (4) the risk of dysrhthymias or ICD shocks [119].
1266	
1267	  When significant debate or doubt occurs regarding the participation of an athlete with an ICD in
1268	competitive sports, consultation should be obtained from medical experts in sports medicine,
1269	cardiomyopathies and ICDs. In athletes where a consensus decision is made that return to play is
1270	desirable and permissible, maximal effort exercise testing should be performed to evaluate for
1271	inducible dysrhythmias prior to sports participation and the treatment of the athlete adjusted if
1272	necessary [120].
1273	
1274	  Athletes with ICDs who do participate in competitive sports often require optimal device-based
1275	tachycardia programming, such as high-rate tachycardia cutoff (200 beats per minute) and long-
1276	detection duration programming [121]. Optimal ICD programing reduces the total and inappropriate
1277	ICD shocks without decreasing athlete survival or increasing the risk of transient loss-of-
1278	consciousness. A remote ICD monitoring plan and an emergency action plan for cardiac events also
1279	should be developed. In addition, the National Collegiate Athletic Association in conjunction with the
1280	American College of Cardiology recommends the presence at sporting events of responders trained in
1281	cardiopulmonary resuscitation and automatic external defibrillator (AED) use, immediate access to
1282	defibrillation devices by sport personnel, and the integration of onsite sport personnel responders with
1283	local emergency medical services [122].
1284	
1285	
1286	  All athletes with ICDs must be carefully followed-up by a physician with prompt intervention when

ACM risk score is available at http://ACMrisk.com [96, 97, 98].

TREATMENT

Restriction of exercise activity is extremely important in the management of individuals with ACM
because restriction of exercise intensity and duration significantly decreases the amount of ventricular
dysrhythmias. Athletes with ACM should be restricted to low level activity such as 30 minutes of brisk
walking per day, because exercise levels >650 MET-hours per year accelerate the phenotypic
expression of ACM [99-101]. Exercise restriction should also be advised in athletes and in family
members who are genotype positive but phenotype negative in order to delay potential phenotypic
expression and should also be considered in athletes with borderline or possible ACM [91,102, 103].

  The use of beta-adrenergic receptor antagonists is recommended in athletes with ACM and non-
sustained ventricular tachycardia or other ventricular dysrhythmias [91]. Adjuvant pharmacotherapy
with flecainide or amiodarone should be considered in athletes with ongoing ventricular dysrhythmias
despite the use of a beta-adrenergic receptor antagonist [104]. However, therapy with beta adrenergic
receptor antagonists, flecainide, amiodarone or ventricular ablation of endocardial/epicardial
ventricular tachycardia foci does not obviate the need for ICDs in high risk athletes as determined by
the ACM risk score [91, 99, 105, 106]. For athletes with asymptomatic but significant RV and/or LV
 reduction in ejection fractions, treatment with angiotensin-converting-enzyme inhibitors or angiotensin
II receptor blockers should also be considered [99].

  The decision to insert an ICD in an athlete for primary preventions requires thorough evaluation of
the risk of sudden cardiac death and the risk of ICD device-related complications, which include a 3.9%
annual rate of shocks and a 4.2% annual rate of complications such as infection or lead malfunction
[107]... In those athletes with a 5% to 15% 5-year risk with a history of aborted cardiac arrest or sudden
cardiac death, sustain ventricular tachycardia, severe RV, LV or biventricular dysfunction, an ICD is
indicated [99, 108, 109]. In those athletes with intermediate risk with >1 major risk factor such as
syncope, non-sustain ventricular tachycardia, moderate ventricular dysfunction, an ICD should be
considered. In those athletes with >I minor risk factors, an ICD may be considered and in those
athletes with <5% 5-year risk, an ICD is not recommended [99, 108, 109]. For athletes undergoing ICD
implantation for primary prevention of ventricular dysrhythmias, a subcutaneous ICD should be
considered whereas for athletes who present with sustained monomorphic VT, an endocardial ICD
device should be considered because of the risk of recurrent sustained dysrhythmias. Finally, athletes
with uncontrollable ventricular tachydysrhythmias or intractable heart failure require evaluation for
heart transplantation [110].

Athletes with ACM require reevaluation every one to two years for new onset or worsening of
symptoms, progression of ventricular myocardial abnormalities, and supraventricular and ventricular
dysrhythmias. In these athletes, the risk of sudden cardiac arrest/death should be re-assessed and
treatment further optimized [99].



ATHLETES WITH IMPLANTABLE CARDIOVERTERS-DEFIBRILLATORS (ICDs)

In individuals of all ages with cardiac disease at high risk for ventricular dysrhythmias, ICDs are
effective in preventing ventricular dysrhythmias and sudden cardiac arrest [84, 107-109, 111-113].
However in the past the AHA/ACC guidelines have recommended against all moderate and high-
intensity sports for athletes with ICDs because the safety and efficacy of these devices during sport
competition was unknown. Recently, studies have reported that athletes primarily with HCM or long
QT syndrome with LV ejection fractions in the normal or the mildly reduced range may be able to
participate safely in noncontact or low contact competitive sports with a low risk of life-threatening
events [113-116]. In these studies appropriate, as well as inappropriate shocks due to T-wave over-
sensing, supraventricular or sinus tachycardia, and lead malfunction, have been reported. A limitation
of some of these studies is that ICD shocks have been self-reported by the athletes or their care givers
and these individuals may have purposefully withheld information about ICD shocks in order to
continue sports participation. Nevertheless, the AHA/ACC currently has Class II recommendations for
athletes with ICDs where participation in sports may be considered if the risk of adverse outcomes
appears to be low or disease-specific management may reduce the risk to acceptable levels [117,118].
 In addition, the European Association of Preventive Cardiology recommends that return to play
decisions be made after thorough discussion and shared decision making by the physician(s) with the
athlete with the ICD, the interested parties (care providers, coaches, institutions and/or organizations)
of the “four Ds”:   (1) the underlying cardiac disease; (2) the danger to the athlete, third parties
involved, and the environment; (3) the device; and (4) the risk of dysrhthymias or ICD shocks [119].

  When significant debate or doubt occurs regarding the participation of an athlete with an ICD in
competitive sports, consultation should be obtained from medical experts in sports medicine,
cardiomyopathies and ICDs. In athletes where a consensus decision is made that return to play is
desirable and permissible, maximal effort exercise testing should be performed to evaluate for
inducible dysrhythmias prior to sports participation and the treatment of the athlete adjusted if
necessary [120].

  Athletes with ICDs who do participate in competitive sports often require optimal device-based
tachycardia programming, such as high-rate tachycardia cutoff (200 beats per minute) and long-
detection duration programming [121]. Optimal ICD programing reduces the total and inappropriate
ICD shocks without decreasing athlete survival or increasing the risk of transient loss-of-
consciousness. A remote ICD monitoring plan and an emergency action plan for cardiac events also
should be developed. In addition, the National Collegiate Athletic Association in conjunction with the
American College of Cardiology recommends the presence at sporting events of responders trained in
cardiopulmonary resuscitation and automatic external defibrillator (AED) use, immediate access to
defibrillation devices by sport personnel, and the integration of onsite sport personnel responders with
local emergency medical services [122].


  All athletes with ICDs must be carefully followed-up by a physician with prompt intervention when
new/novel symptoms occur or worsening of the underlying heart disease occurs. In addition, ongoing
assessment by a physician of the psychologic needs of the athlete with an ICD is an important
component of management. Athlete anxiety and depression can significantly increase after a single or
multiple ICD shocks [123,124].



SUMMARY AND CONCLUSIONS

There are currently 5 million active high school, collegiate, professional, and master athletes in the
United States. Regular intense exercise by these athletes can promote structural, electrical and
functional remodeling of the hearts termed the “athlete’s heart.”      Regular intense exercise by an
athlete can also lead to pathological adaptions that can promote or worsen cardiac disease.
Physicians must therefore be aware of the normal cardiac anatomy and physiology of the athlete, the
differentiation of the normal athlete heart from the athlete with cardiomyopathy, and the contemporary
care of the athlete with cardiomyopathy. The distinction between physiologic changes and pathologic
 changes in the hearts of athletes has important prognostic and therapeutic implications. Failure by the
physician to correctly diagnose an athlete with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, dilated cardiomyopathy,
or arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy can lead to sudden cardiac arrest and death in an
athlete during training or competition. Furthermore, an incorrect diagnosis by a physician of cardiac
pathology in an athlete can lead to an unnecessary restriction of athlete training and competition with
resultant significant athlete emotional, psychological, financial, and long-term health consequences.
All athletes with cardiomyopathies must be carefully followed by a physician with prompt intervention

780	  The prevalence of HCM in the United States is approximately 1:200 to 1:500 Americans [55]. This
781	suggests that as many as 750,000 Americans can be affected by HCM. However, only a small fraction
782	of the American population are actually diagnosed with HCM even though in the United States HCM is
783	the single most common cause of deaths among athletes [55, 56]. Testing for HCM genes MYH7,
784	MYBPC3, TNNI3, TNNT2, TPM1, MYL2, MYL3, and ACTC1 is helpful in athletes with possible HCM and,
785	if positive, first degree relatives should be tested for HCM [57].
786	   Transthoracic echocardiography is the most readily accessible and informative imaging technique
787	for diagnosing HCM. In athletes with HCM, echocardiography provides quantitative measurements of
788	the size and the location of the ventricular hypertrophy, provides assessment of any mitral valve-
789	interventricular septum subaortic obstruction, characterizes the magnitude of mitral valve
790	regurgitation, and estimates pulmonary artery systolic pressures. Echocardiographic measurements of
791	LV wall thickness should be performed at end-diastole, preferably in short-axis views and all LV
792	segments from base to apex should be examined with the wall thickness recorded at the mitral, mid-
793	LV, and apical levels. In an adult, HCM is defined by a wall thickness ≥15 mm in one or more LV
794	myocardial segments [57]. However, elite athletes participating in sports with high static and mixed
795	sports can display profound LV remodeling that can be confused with HCM [38, 56]. Nevertheless, the
796	presence of systolic anterior motion of the mitral valve against the interventricular system with a LV
797	outflow tract (LVOT) pressure gradient is inconsistent with a diagnosis of athlete‘s heart and strongly
798	suggests HCM in the athlete [55,57].
799	
800	   The LV outflow tract obstruction in HCM is caused by asymmetrical septal hypertrophy, an
801	elongated mitral valve anterior leaflet which is often >30 mm in diameter (17 mm/m2), apically displaced
802	hypertrophied papillary muscles that tether the mitral valve apparatus toward the interventricular
803	septum, and anterior motion of the mitral valve against the interventricular septum in mid-systole with
804	>30% systolic contact [57]. See FIGURE 5.

812	General Hospital Echocardiographic Department.

815	Hg at rest and with exercise termed nonobstructive HCM.         Alternatively, athletes may have LVOT
816	obstruction at rest with gradients ≥30 mm Hg, or pressure gradients ≥30 mm Hg with exercise or
817	pharmacologic provocation which is termed obstructive HCM.
818

820	decreasing LV filling and increasing the anterior mitral valve leaflet-interventricular septal contact.

MBA5




 Abstract
 Background: This study aimed to determine the relationship of recovery
 period length on overall injury patterns (rates and incidence) for athletes in
 the National Football League.
 Methods: Official NFL gamebooks were queried from 2011 to 2015,
 and each in-game injury was analyzed for all regular season games. Data
 included athlete name, position, season, week, date, weekday, teams, and
 injured body part. ANOVA testing determined statistical significance of
 injury rates across weekdays, season weeks, and positions.
 Results: A total of 27,712 injuries were analyzed. On average, 21.4 (8.6;
 20.9-21.9) injuries were sustained per game on Sunday, 18.2 (6.9; 16.7-
 19.7) on Monday, and 21.7 (6.9; 20.2-23.3) on Thursday. The difference
 between Sunday and Thursday games was negligible (p=0.9264), while
 Monday games had fewer injuries than Sundays (p=0.0028) and Thursdays
 (p=0.0214). There was no difference in number of injuries each team
 sustained on Thursday compared to the week prior to (10.8 versus 10.8;
 p= 0.4971) or week after (10.8 versus 10.7; p=0.7315) its Thursday game.         Affiliation:

4	Jose R. Perez,*† MD, Jonathan Burke,‡ MPH, Abdul K. Zalikha,‡ MD, Dhanur Damodar,† MD,

10	Background: Although claims of increased injury rates with Thursday night National Football League (NFL) games exist, a paucity
11	of data exist substantiating these claims.
12	Purpose: To evaluate the effect of rest between games on in-game injury rates as it pertains to overall injury incidence, location,
13	and player position.
14	Study Design: Descriptive epidemiologic study.
15	Methods: Data were obtained from official NFL game books for regular season games from all 32 teams for the 2013-2016
16	seasons. All in-game injuries recorded in official game books were included. Rest periods between games were classified as
17	short (4 days), regular (6-8 days), or long (10 days). Overall observed injury rates per team-game were analyzed in relation to
18	different rest periods using negative binomial regression. For results with significant overall findings, pairwise comparisons were
19	tested using the Wald chi-square test. Exploratory secondary analyses were performed in a similar fashion to assess differences in
20	injury rates for the different rest periods when stratified by anatomic location and player position.
21	Results: A total of 2846 injuries were identified throughout the 4 seasons. There was an overall significant difference in injuries per
22	team-game between short, regular, and long rest (P ¼ .01). With short rest, an observed mean of 1.26 injuries per game (95% CI,
23	1.06-1.49) was significantly different from the 1.53 observed injuries per game with regular rest (95% CI, 1.46-1.60; P ¼ .03), but not
24	compared with the 1.34 observed injuries per game with long rest (P ¼ .56). For player position, only the tight end, linebacker, and
25	fullback group demonstrated significant differences between the injury rates for different rest categories. Quarterback was the only
26	position with more injuries during games played on Thursday compared with both regular and long rest. This specific analysis was
27	underpowered and the difference was not significant (P ¼ .08). No differences were found regarding injury rates in correlation with
28	differences in rest periods with different injury locations.
29	Conclusion: A short rest period between games is not associated with increased rates of observed injuries reported in NFL game
30	books; rather, our data suggest there are significantly fewer injuries for Thursday night games compared with games played on
31	regular rest. Future research correlating rest and quarterback injury rates is warranted.

The Effect of Thursday Night Games
on In-Game Injury Rates in the
National Football League
Jose R. Perez,*† MD, Jonathan Burke,‡ MPH, Abdul K. Zalikha,‡ MD, Dhanur Damodar,† MD,
Joseph S. Geller,‡ BA, Andrew N.L. Buskard,† PhD, Lee D. Kaplan,† MD,
and Michael G. Baraga,† MD
Investigation performed at University of Miami Sports Medicine Institute,
University of Miami Miller School of Medicine, Miami, Florida, USA

Background: Although claims of increased injury rates with Thursday night National Football League (NFL) games exist, a paucity
of data exist substantiating these claims.
Purpose: To evaluate the effect of rest between games on in-game injury rates as it pertains to overall injury incidence, location,
and player position.
Study Design: Descriptive epidemiologic study.
Methods: Data were obtained from official NFL game books for regular season games from all 32 teams for the 2013-2016
seasons. All in-game injuries recorded in official game books were included. Rest periods between games were classified as
short (4 days), regular (6-8 days), or long (10 days). Overall observed injury rates per team-game were analyzed in relation to
different rest periods using negative binomial regression. For results with significant overall findings, pairwise comparisons were
tested using the Wald chi-square test. Exploratory secondary analyses were performed in a similar fashion to assess differences in
injury rates for the different rest periods when stratified by anatomic location and player position.
Results: A total of 2846 injuries were identified throughout the 4 seasons. There was an overall significant difference in injuries per
team-game between short, regular, and long rest (P ¼ .01). With short rest, an observed mean of 1.26 injuries per game (95% CI,
1.06-1.49) was significantly different from the 1.53 observed injuries per game with regular rest (95% CI, 1.46-1.60; P ¼ .03), but not
compared with the 1.34 observed injuries per game with long rest (P ¼ .56). For player position, only the tight end, linebacker, and
fullback group demonstrated significant differences between the injury rates for different rest categories. Quarterback was the only
position with more injuries during games played on Thursday compared with both regular and long rest. This specific analysis was
underpowered and the difference was not significant (P ¼ .08). No differences were found regarding injury rates in correlation with
differences in rest periods with different injury locations.
Conclusion: A short rest period between games is not associated with increased rates of observed injuries reported in NFL game
books; rather, our data suggest there are significantly fewer injuries for Thursday night games compared with games played on
regular rest. Future research correlating rest and quarterback injury rates is warranted.
Keywords: football (American); epidemiology; general sports trauma; injury prevention

 "id":"Q56",
 "sourceFile":"The effect of Thursday night games on in-game injury rates in the National Football League.pdf",
 "decision":"INCLUDE",
 "exclusionReason":"",
 "degradedReason":"",
 "doiMissing":false,
 "identityCheck":"Title in text is 'The Effect of Thursday Night Games on In-Game Injury Rates in the National Football League', matching the filename.",
 "confidence":"high",
 "studyDesign":"Cross-sectional Study",
 "primaryDomain":"Sports Medicine & Injury",
 "domains":["Sports Medicine & Injury","Recovery & Readiness"],
 "audiences":["Sports Medicine","Athletic Training","Performance"],
 "sports":["American Football"],
 "populations":["Professional / Elite","Injured Athletes"],
 "evidenceSummary":"Descriptive epidemiologic study using official NFL game books for regular-season games from the 2013 to 2016 seasons, covering 2,846 in-game injuries. Negative binomial regression compared injuries per team-game across short (4 days, 128 games), regular (6 to 8 days, 1,530 games) and long (10 or more days, 262 games) rest. Injury rates were 1.26, 1.53 and 1.34 per team-game respectively, with short rest lower than regular rest (P = .03) but not different from long rest (P = .56), and an overall difference across rest categories (P = .01).",
 "screeningLimitations":"The game books record injuries for media coverage, so minor injuries that do not stop play may be missed, and the team-game analysis is unadjusted. The quarterback subgroup was underpowered (power 0.50), and the design cannot show that rest causes the observed differences.",
 "synthesisCaution":"Staff could take the finding of fewer injuries after short rest as evidence that short weeks protect players, when the authors say shortened rest may reduce preparedness, recovery and performance even though injury counts did not rise, and the lower rate was seen only against regular rest.",
 "paper":{
   "year":2020,
   "citation":"Perez JR, Burke J, Zalikha AK, et al. The Effect of Thursday Night Games on In-Game Injury Rates in the National Football League. The American Journal of Sports Medicine. 2020;48(8):1999-2003.",
   "doi":"10.1177/0363546520919989",
   "abstract":"Used official NFL game book records of in-game injuries for regular-season games from 2013 to 2016 to compare injury rates across short, regular and long rest between games. Injuries were lower after short rest than after regular rest, and not different from long rest. Quarterbacks had a non-significant rise in injuries on Thursday games.",
   "tldr":"In NFL game-book data from 2013 to 2016, short rest before a game was not linked to more in-game injuries than regular rest, and it was linked to fewer. Quarterbacks showed a non-significant rise on short rest that needs more study.",
   "methods":"Descriptive epidemiologic study of in-game injuries from official NFL game books for all 32 teams in the 2013 to 2016 regular seasons. Rest periods were classed as short (4 days), regular (6 to 8 days) and long (10 or more days). Injuries per team-game were analysed with negative binomial regression, Wald chi-square pairwise tests, and exploratory analyses by position and injury location.",
   "findings":"There were 2,846 injuries in total. Injuries per team-game were 1.26 after short rest (95% CI 1.06 to 1.49), 1.53 after regular rest (95% CI 1.46 to 1.60) and 1.34 after long rest (95% CI 1.19 to 1.50). Short rest differed from regular rest (P = .03) but not from long rest (P = .56), and the overall test was significant (P = .01). Only the high-impact position group (tight end, fullback, linebacker) differed across rest categories (overall P = .005), and quarterbacks had 0.08 injuries per game on Thursdays against 0.05 on regular rest (non-significant).",
   "limitations":"The authors note that game books are kept for media coverage, so injuries that stop play are more likely to be recorded than minor injuries, and players who rotate in and out often, such as special teams players, may be under-reported. The analyses are unadjusted, the quarterback analysis was underpowered (power 0.50), and the quarterback difference is reported as P = .08 in the abstract and P = .16 in the discussion. The study did not link rest to mechanism or severity.",
   "practicalImplications":"Staff should not assume that short weeks increase in-game injury counts, based on these data, but they should watch quarterbacks on short rest, where the authors saw a non-significant rise. The authors call for work that links rest to injury mechanisms, and their follow-up study was planned to address this.",
   "athleteDev":"Performance Application: These data suggest that short rest did not raise in-game injury counts in this sample, but the authors note that short rest may still reduce preparedness, recovery and performance. The study did not measure those outcomes, so staff should track them directly rather than infer them from injury counts.",
   "rtp":"Return to Sport Application: The study counts in-game injuries at the team level and does not examine return-to-play timing, re-injury or individual clearance. It cannot be used to decide when an injured player should return after a short week, although its finding of no association between rest and injury type, including concussion, is a team-level result only."
 }
}

 "paper":{

   "citation":"Clarke R, Read PJ, De Ste Croix MBA, Hughes JD. The deceleration deficit: a novel field-based method to quantify deceleration during change of direction performance. Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research. 2022;36(9):2434-2439.",
   "doi":"",
   "abstract":"Examined relationships between linear sprint, 505 change of direction time, change of direction deficit (CODD) and a new deceleration deficit (DD) in 36 athletes who performed 505 trials in both turning directions and 15 m sprints. Linear speed correlated with 505 time but not with CODD or DD, DD correlated moderately with CODD, and most athletes had a worthwhile difference between the two deficit measures.",
   "tldr":"The deceleration deficit is a field-based way to separate braking ability from linear speed in the 505 test. Coaches may find it useful for individualising training, but it still needs validity and reliability testing.",
   "methods":"Cross-sectional design in which participants completed three 505 trials in each turning direction and three 15 m linear sprints in one session. DD was calculated as full approach time in the 505 minus the 15 m sprint time, and CODD as 505 time minus 10 m sprint time. Pearson correlations and within-person z-score comparisons with a moderate worthwhile change threshold were used.",
   "findings":"Linear 10 m and 15 m sprint times correlated with 505 time (dominant r = 0.71 and 0.74; non-dominant r = 0.76 and 0.75; all p < 0.01). Linear sprint times were not significantly related to CODD or DD. DD correlated with CODD (dominant r = 0.59, non-dominant r = 0.62; both p < 0.01). Of the participants, 78% had a difference between CODD and DD z-scores greater than the moderate worthwhile change in at least one turning direction.",
   "limitations":"The authors state that DD requires validity and reliability testing, and that most of its correlations with other measures were below r = 0.5, so most of DD's variance is not explained by them. The methods describe participants as recreationally active, while the discussion calls them competitive university-level athletes. Sample size was small and drawn from mixed invasion sports, and DD was not compared against force-plate measures.",
   "practicalImplications":"Coaches could compare DD with CODD to see whether an athlete's change of direction time is limited by braking or by linear speed in each turning direction. The 505 test and a 15 m sprint can be done with timing gates, but DD should be checked with reliability testing in the squad before it guides individual programmes.",
   "athleteDev":"Performance Application: Coaches can use DD alongside linear speed and CODD to decide whether an athlete needs braking work or linear speed work, and to compare the two turning directions.    "rtp":"Return to Sport Application: The study did not include injured athletes or any return-to-play measures, so it cannot be used to judge readiness to return after injury or to set return-to-sport criteria for braking or change of direction."
